verses.zh: 「以后，我们转回，向巴珊去。巴珊王噩和他的众民都出来，在以得来与我们交战。
verses.en: Next we set out on[NOTE:1] the route to Bashan,[NOTE:2] but King Og of Bashan and his whole army[NOTE:3] came out to meet us in battle at Edrei.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “turned and went up.”
Bashan. This plateau country, famous for its oaks (Isa 2:13) and cattle (Deut 32:14; Amos 4:1), was north of Gilead along the Yarmuk River.
Heb “people.”
Edrei is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see Num 21:33; Josh 12:4; 13:12, 31; also mentioned in Deut 1:4).

verses.zh: 耶和华对我说：『不要怕他！因我已将他和他的众民，并他的地，都交在你手中；你要待他像从前待住希实本的亚摩利王西宏一样。』
verses.en: The Lord, however, said to me, “Don’t be afraid of him because I have already given him, his whole army,[NOTE:1] and his land to you. You will do to him exactly what you did to King Sihon of the Amorites who lived in Heshbon.”
notes: Heb “people.”

verses.zh: 于是耶和华―我们的　神也将巴珊王噩和他的众民都交在我们手中；我们杀了他们，没有留下一个。
verses.en: So the Lord our God did indeed give over to us King Og of Bashan and his whole army, and we struck them down until not a single survivor was left.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “was left to him.” The final phrase “to him” is redundant in English and has been left untranslated.

verses.zh: 那时，我们夺了他所有的城，共有六十座，没有一座城不被我们所夺。这为亚珥歌伯的全境，就是巴珊地噩王的国。
verses.en: We captured all his cities at that time—there was not a town we did not take from them—sixty cities, all the region of Argob,[NOTE:1] the dominion of Og in Bashan.
notes: Argob. This is a subdistrict of Bashan, perhaps north of the Yarmuk River. See Y. Aharoni, Land of the Bible, 314.

verses.zh: 这些城都有坚固的高墙，有门有闩。此外还有许多无城墙的乡村。
verses.en: All of these cities were fortified by high walls, gates, and locking bars;[NOTE:1] in addition there were a great many open villages.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “high walls and barred gates” (NLT); Heb “high walls, gates, and bars.” Since “bars” could be understood to mean “saloons,” the qualifying adjective “locking” has been supplied in the translation.
The Hebrew term פְּרָזִי (perazi) refers to rural areas, at the most “unwalled villages” (KJV, NASB “unwalled towns”).

verses.zh: 我们将这些都毁灭了，像从前待希实本王西宏一样，把有人烟的各城，连女人带孩子，尽都毁灭；
verses.en: We put all of these under divine judgment[NOTE:1] just as we had done to King Sihon of Heshbon—every occupied city,[NOTE:2] including women and children.
notes: The divine curse. See note on this phrase in Deut 2:34.tn Heb “we put them under the ban” (נַחֲרֵם, nakharem). See note at 2:34.
Heb “city of men.”

verses.zh: 惟有一切牲畜和城中的财物都取为自己的掠物。
verses.en: But all the livestock and plunder from the cities we kept for ourselves.

verses.zh: 那时，我们从约旦河东两个亚摩利王的手将亚嫩谷直到黑门山之地夺过来
verses.en: So at that time we took the land of the two Amorite kings in the Transjordan from Wadi Arnon to Mount Hermon[NOTE:1]
notes: Mount Hermon. This is the famous peak at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range known today as Jebel es-Sheik.

verses.zh: （这黑门山，西顿人称为西连，亚摩利人称为示尼珥），
verses.en: (the Sidonians[NOTE:1] call Hermon Sirion[NOTE:2] and the Amorites call it Senir),[NOTE:3]
notes: Sidonians were Phoenician inhabitants of the city of Sidon (now in Lebanon), about 47 mi (75 km) north of Mount Carmel.
Sirion. This name is attested in the Ugaritic texts as sryn. See UT 495.

Senir. Probably this was actually one of the peaks of Hermon and not the main mountain (Song of Songs 4:8; 1 Chr 5:23). It is mentioned in a royal inscription of Shalmaneser III of Assyria (saniru; see ANET 280).

verses.zh: 就是夺了平原的各城、基列全地、巴珊全地，直到撒迦和以得来，都是巴珊王噩国内的城邑。
verses.en: all the cities of the plateau, all of Gilead and Bashan as far as Salecah[NOTE:1] and Edrei,[NOTE:2] cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.
notes: Salecah. Today this is known as Salkhad, in Jordan, about 31 mi (50 km) east of the Jordan River in the Hauran Desert.
Edrei. See note on this term in 3:1.

verses.zh: （利乏音人所剩下的只有巴珊王噩。他的床是铁的，长九肘，宽四肘，都是以人肘为度。现今岂不是在亚扪人的拉巴吗？）」
verses.en: Only King Og of Bashan was left of the remaining Rephaites. (It is noteworthy[NOTE:1] that his sarcophagus[NOTE:2] was made of iron.[NOTE:3] Does it not, indeed, still remain in Rabbath[NOTE:4] of the Ammonites? It is 13½ feet[NOTE:5] long and 6 feet[NOTE:6] wide according to standard measure.)[NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “Behold” (הִנֵּה, hinneh).

The Hebrew term עֶרֶשׂ (ʿeres), traditionally translated “bed” (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT) is likely a basaltic (volcanic) stone sarcophagus of suitable size to contain the coffin of the giant Rephaite king. Its iron-like color and texture caused it to be described as an iron container. See A. Millard, “King Og’s Iron Bed: Fact or Fancy?” BR 6 (1990): 16-21, 44; cf. also NEB “his sarcophagus of basalt”; TEV, CEV “his coffin.”
Or “of iron-colored basalt.” See note on the word “sarcophagus” earlier in this verse.

Rabbath. This place name (usually occurring as Rabbah; 2 Sam 11:11; 12:27; Jer 49:3) refers to the ancient capital of the Ammonite kingdom, now the modern city of Amman, Jordan. The word means “great [one],” probably because of its political importance. The fact that the sarcophagus “still remain[ed]” there suggests this part of the verse is post-Mosaic, having been added as a matter of explanation for the existence of the artifact and also to verify the claim as to its size.
Heb “9 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 in (45 cm) for the standard cubit, this would be 13.5 ft (4.1 m) long.
Heb “4 cubits.” This would be 6 ft (1.8 m) wide.
Heb “by the cubit of man.” This probably refers to the “short” or “regular” cubit of approximately 18 in (45 cm).

verses.zh: 「那时，我们得了这地。从亚嫩谷边的亚罗珥起，我将基列山地的一半，并其中的城邑，都给了流便人和迦得人。
verses.en: This is the land we brought under our control at that time: The territory extending from Aroer[NOTE:1] by the Wadi Arnon and half the Gilead hill country with its cities I gave to the Reubenites and Gadites.[NOTE:2]
notes: The words “the territory extending” are not in the Hebrew text; they are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.sn Aroer. See note on this term in Deut 2:36.

Reubenites and Gadites. By the time of Moses’ address the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh had already been granted permission to settle in the Transjordan, provided they helped the other tribes subdue the occupants of Canaan (cf. Num 32:28-42).

verses.zh: 其余的基列地和巴珊全地，就是噩王的国，我给了玛拿西半支派。亚珥歌伯全地乃是巴珊全地；这叫做利乏音人之地。
verses.en: The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to half the tribe of Manasseh.[NOTE:1] (All the region of Argob,[NOTE:2] that is, all Bashan, is called the land of Rephaim.
notes: Half the tribe of Manasseh. The tribe of Manasseh split into clans, with half opting to settle in Bashan and the other half in Canaan (cf. Num 32:39-42; Josh 17:1-13).
Argob. See note on this term in v. 4.

verses.zh: 玛拿西的子孙睚珥占了亚珥歌伯全境，直到基述人和玛迦人的交界，就按自己的名称这巴珊地为哈倭特・睚珥，直到今日。
verses.en: Jair, son of Manasseh, took all the Argob region as far as the border with the Geshurites[NOTE:1] and Maacathites[NOTE:2]—namely Bashan—and called it by his name, Havvoth Jair,[NOTE:3] which it retains to this very day.)
notes: Geshurites. Geshur was a city and its surrounding area somewhere northeast of Bashan (cf. Josh 12:5 ; 13:11, 13). One of David’s wives was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur and mother of Absalom (cf. 2 Sam 13:37; 15:8; 1 Chr 3:2).

Maacathites. These were the people of a territory southwest of Mount Hermon on the Jordan River. The name probably has nothing to do with David’s wife from Geshur (see note on “Geshurites” earlier in this verse).
Havvoth Jair. The Hebrew name means “villages of Jair,” the latter being named after a son (i.e., descendant) of Manasseh who took the area by conquest.

verses.zh: 我又将基列给了玛吉。
verses.en: I gave Gilead to Machir.[NOTE:1]
notes: Machir was the name of another descendant of Manasseh (cf. Num 32:41; 1 Chr 7:14-19). Eastern Manasseh was thus divided between the Jairites and the Machirites.

verses.zh: 从基列到亚嫩谷，以谷中为界，直到亚扪人交界的雅博河，我给了流便人和迦得人，
verses.en: To the Reubenites and Gadites I allocated the territory extending from Gilead as far as Wadi Arnon (the exact middle of the wadi was a boundary) all the way to the Wadi Jabbok, the Ammonite border.

verses.zh: 又将亚拉巴和靠近约旦河之地，从基尼烈直到亚拉巴海，就是盐海，并毗斯迦山根东边之地，都给了他们。
verses.en: The rift valley[NOTE:1] and the Jordan River[NOTE:2] were also a border, from the Sea of Kinnereth[NOTE:3] to the sea of the rift valley (that is, the Salt Sea),[NOTE:4] beneath the slopes[NOTE:5] of Pisgah[NOTE:6] to the east.
notes: The rift valley extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The Jordan River runs through it from Galilee to the Dead Sea, so the rift valley, the Jordan, and the Dead Sea work together naturally as a boundary.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity (also in vv. 20, 25).

Kinnereth. This is another name for the Sea of Galilee, so called because its shape is that of a harp (the Hebrew term for “harp” is כִּנּוֹר, kinnor).tn Heb “from Kinnereth.” The words “the sea of” have been supplied in the translation as a clarification.
The Salt Sea is another name for the Dead Sea (cf. Gen 14:3; Josh 3:16).
The slopes (אֲשֵׁדוֹת, ʾashedot) refer to the ascent from the rift valley, generally in the region of the Dead Sea, up to the flatlands (or wilderness).

Pisgah. This appears to refer to a small range of mountains, the most prominent peak of which is Mount Nebo (Num 21:20; 23:14; Deut 3:27; cf. 34:1). Pisgah is east of the northern tip of the Dead Sea. The slopes ascend approximately 3600 feet from the Dead Sea to Pisgah, while the plains to the east lie only a few hundred feet below these heights.

verses.zh: 「那时，我吩咐你们说：『耶和华―你们的　神已将这地赐给你们为业；你们所有的勇士都要带着兵器，在你们的弟兄以色列人前面过去。
verses.en: At that time I instructed you as follows: “The Lord your God has given you this land for your possession. You warriors are to cross over equipped for battle before your fellow Israelites.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “your brothers, the sons of Israel.”

verses.zh: 但你们的妻子、孩子、牲畜（我知道你们有许多的牲畜）可以住在我所赐给你们的各城里。
verses.en: But your wives, children, and livestock (of which I know you have many) may remain in the cities I have given you.

verses.zh: 等到你们弟兄在约旦河那边，也得耶和华―你们　神所赐给他们的地，又使他们得享平安，与你们一样，你们才可以回到我所赐给你们为业之地。』
verses.en: You must fight[NOTE:1] until the Lord gives your countrymen victory[NOTE:2] as he did you and they take possession of the land that the Lord your God is giving them on the other side of the Jordan River. Then each of you may return to his own territory that I have given you.”
notes: The words “you must fight” are not present in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “gives your brothers rest.”

verses.zh: 那时我吩咐约书亚说：『你亲眼看见了耶和华―你　神向这二王所行的；耶和华也必向你所要去的各国照样行。
verses.en: I also commanded Joshua at the same time, “You have seen everything the Lord your God did to these two kings; he[NOTE:1] will do the same to all the kingdoms where you are going.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the Lord.” The translation uses the pronoun (“he”) for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.
Heb “which you are crossing over there.”

verses.zh: 你不要怕他们，因那为你争战的是耶和华―你的　神。』」
verses.en: Do not be afraid of them, for the Lord your God will personally fight for you.”

verses.zh: 「那时，我恳求耶和华说：
verses.en: Moreover, at that time I pleaded with the Lord,

verses.zh: 『主耶和华啊，你已将你的大力大能显给仆人看。在天上，在地下，有甚么　神能像你行事、像你有大能的作为呢？
verses.en: “O, Sovereign Lord,[NOTE:1] you have begun to show me[NOTE:2] your greatness and strength.[NOTE:3] (What god in heaven or earth can rival your works and mighty deeds?)
notes: Heb “Lord Yahweh.” The phrase אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (ʾadonay yehvih) is customarily rendered by Jewish tradition as “Lord God.”
Heb “your servant.” The pronoun is used in the translation to clarify that Moses is speaking of himself, since in contemporary English one does not usually refer to oneself in third person.
Heb “your strong hand” (so NIV), a symbol of God’s activity.

verses.zh: 求你容我过去，看约旦河那边的美地，就是那佳美的山地和黎巴嫩。』
verses.en: Let me please cross over to see the good land on the other side of the Jordan River—this good hill country and the Lebanon!”[NOTE:1]
notes: The article is retained in the translation (“the Lebanon,” cf. also NAB, NRSV) to indicate that a region (rather than the modern country of Lebanon) is referred to here. Other recent English versions accomplish this by supplying “mountains” after “Lebanon” (TEV, CEV, NLT).

verses.zh: 但耶和华因你们的缘故向我发怒，不应允我，对我说：『罢了！你不要向我再提这事。
verses.en: But the Lord was angry at me because of you and would not listen to me. Instead, he[NOTE:1] said to me, “Enough of that![NOTE:2] Do not speak to me anymore about this matter.
notes: Heb “the Lord.” For stylistic reasons the pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation here.
Heb “much to you” (an idiom).

verses.zh: 你且上毗斯迦山顶去，向东、西、南、北举目观望，因为你必不能过这约旦河。
verses.en: Go up to the top of Pisgah and take a good look to the west, north, south, and east,[NOTE:1] for you will not be allowed to cross the Jordan.
notes: Heb “lift your eyes to the west, north, south, and east and see with your eyes.” The translation omits the repetition of “your eyes” for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 你却要嘱咐约书亚，勉励他，使他胆壮；因为他必在这百姓前面过去，使他们承受你所要观看之地。』
verses.en: Commission[NOTE:1] Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, because he will lead these people over and will enable them to inherit the land you will see.”
notes: Heb “command”; KJV, NASB, NRSV “charge Joshua.”

verses.zh: 于是我们住在伯・毗珥对面的谷中。」
verses.en: So we settled down in the valley opposite Beth Peor.[NOTE:1]
notes: Beth Peor. This is probably the spot near Pisgah where Balaam attempted to curse the nation Israel (Num 23:28). The Moabites also worshiped Baal there by the name “Baal [of] Peor” (Num 25:1-5).

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: DEUTERONOMY 3:1-7

1"Then we turned and went up the road to Bashan, and Og, king of Bashan,
with all his people came out to meet us in battle at Edrei. 2But the Lord said to me, 'Do not fear him,
for I have delivered him and all his people and his land into your hand; and you shall do to him just as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who
lived at Heshbon.' 3So the Lord our God delivered Og also, king of Bashan, with all his people into our
hand, and we smote them until no survivor was left. 4We captured all his cities at that time; there was not a city which we did not take
from them: sixty cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. 5All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates and
bars, besides a great many unwalled towns. 6We utterly destroyed them, as we did to Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men,
women and children of every city. 7But all the animals and the spoil of the cities we took as our booty."

3:1 "up. . .road" This refers to the King's Highway. This was a trans-Jordan road which went directly
through the center of Edom, Moab, and Ammon. It was a major caravan route from the Gulf of Aqaba to Damascus
(see full note at Deut. 2:1).

▣ "Bashan" The name means "smooth" (BDB 143), in the sense of prime agricultural land (i.e. no rocks). This
was a very fertile and wooded land in the northern trans-Jordan area north of the Yarmuk River or possibly Jabbok River to
just south of the foothills of Mt. Hermon, which means it included part of the area known as Gilead. It was known for its
timber and large herds of cattle.

▣ "Og, king of Bashan" See Num. 21:33-35; Deut. 1:4. He is not mentioned in any ANE text outside the Bible.

▣ "at Edrei" This city (BDB 204) is located on a fork of the Yarmuk River and was one of the royal residences. The
capital was Ashtaroth to the north. Og faced Israel here, probably using the river as a defensive position.

3:2 "the Lord said to me" See note at Deut. 2:2.

▣ "Do not fear him" The VERB (BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense) is used often in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:19,21,29; 2:4; 3:2,22; 4:10). YHWH was
fighting in their behalf (i.e. holy war, e.g. Num. 21:34; Josh. 10:8; 11:6).

▣

NASB, NKJV, REB, Peshitta
"I have delivered him"

NRSV
"I have handed him over to you"

TEV
"I am going to give him"

NJB
"I have put him at your mercy"

LXX
"I have given him over into

your hands"

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT) means "give,"
"put," or "set." It is a common VERB. Notice its use in this literary unit of Deuteronomy
(cf. Deut. 1:8,15,20,21,25,27,35,36,39; 2:5,9,12,19,24,25, 28,29,30,31,33,36; 3:2,3,12,13,15,16,18,19,20; 4:1,8,21,38,40).
YHWH is the giver. There is only one God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣ "we smote them until no survivor was left" This is the language and reality of "holy war." This
reflects the Hebrew concept of herem, or "under the ban" (cf. Deut. 3:6). The following is a representative
sample of OT references to this term which shows how it was used in different ways. The concept of herem
or "holy war," "ban," or "corban":

- total destruction-nothing that breathes is left alive, nothing material can be taken out (cf. Deut. 20:16-18;
1 Sam. 15:3; Joshua 7)

- kill all the people, but leave the cattle (cf. Deut. 2:34, 35; 3:6, 7)

- kill only the men (cf. Deut. 20:10-15)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CURSE

3:4 "region of Argob" The term "region" (BDB 286) literally means, "a cord," it is used of:

- a cord rope

- a measuring line

- a piece of land (i.e. region, cf. Josh. 17:5, or inheritance, cf. Deut. 32:9; Josh. 17:14)

- a group of people (i.e. band of prophets, cf. 1 Sam. 10:5,10)

▣ "Argob" This term (BDB 918) is the name of a region or plot of land. Its location is in the
land of Bashan (cf. Deut. 3:4,13,14; 1 Kgs. 4:13). The root may be related to "clod" (BDB 918) or "heap" (BDB 918),
but this is uncertain.

3:5 "All these cities were fortified with high walls, gates and bars" These cities were built from volcanic rock
blocks and were quite large. They presented a rather intimidating sight. Their size may have reflected the population
of the race of people living there. However, the faith of the Israelites was stronger than their fear of the giants (cf. Deut. 2:20-24).

The Handbook for Translators on Deuteronomy from the United Bible Societies mentions that "gates and bars"
probably refers to a double gate with a metal bar across both, pp. 68-69. This may explain the PLURAL "gates":

- PLURAL as imagery for "strength"

- there may just be more than one gate

- this may have been the characteristic inner and outer gates (i.e. chambers)

3:6

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta
"utterly destroyed"

TEV
"destroyed"

NJB
"the curse of destruction"

REB
"under solemn ban"

JPSOA
"doomed"

This VERB (BDB 355, KB 353) is used twice in this verse (Hiphil
IMPERATIVE and Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE). Its basic meaning is to
devote something to YHWH whereby it becomes too holy for human use and must be destroyed. It is regularly
used in "holy war" contexts (cf. Deut. 2:34; 7:1-2; Exod. 22:20; Josh. 6:17,21) to assert that the victory and, thereby
the spoils belong to YHWH. In these conquest contexts the things devoted to God are the Canaanites and their
property. They are judged because of their abominable sins and unwillingness to repent (cf. Gen. 15:16;
Lev. 18:24-26; Deut. 9:5).

For a good discussion of "holy war" see Ancient Israel, by Roland deVaux, vol. 1, pp. 258-267.

SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: DEUTERONOMY 3:8-11

8"Thus we took the land at that time from the hand of the two kings of
the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the valley of Arnon to Mount Hermon 9(Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and
the Amorites call it Senir): 10all the cities of the plateau and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of
the kingdom of Og in Bashan. 11(For only Og king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bedstead
was an iron bedstead; it is in Rabbah of the sons of Ammon. Its length was nine cubits and its width four cubits by ordinary cubit.)

3:8 "Thus we took the land. . .from the hand of the two kings" Verse 24 says it was "the strong hand of God,"
which, anthropomorphically (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED
AS HUMAN) shows the power and might of God. Here again is the interplay between God's sovereignty and human effort.

▣ "Mount Hermon" Mount Hermon (BDB 249 CONSTRUCT BDB 356) was the northern
limit of the land that YHWH gave to the Israelites. It is the largest mountain in the entire area located in Lebanon, north of the
Sea of Chinnereth (i.e. Galilee). Its name (BDB 356) is related to herem (devoted thing) and the site of many temples
(cf. Ancient Israel, Roland deVaux, vol. 1, pp. 279-282). It is the northern limit of the conquered lands (cf. Jdgs. 1:1).

3:9 "Sidonians" This (BDB 851) was the name of a major city in ancient Phoenicia (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:31). It was located
on the coast north of Tyre, which later became the major city. It being mentioned instead of Tyre shows the ancientness of this text.

▣ "Sirion" This term (BDB 976, Ps. 29:6) used for Mt. Hermon has been found in Ugaritic texts also
shows the ancientness of this text.

▣ "Senir" This term (BDB 972, cf. 1 Chr. 5:23; Song of Songs 4:8; Ezek. 27:5) has been found in
accounts of Shalmaneser III, an Assyrian king who attacked Damascus. It is the Amorite name for Mt. Hermon.

This term (BDB 449) means "a level place." It could refer to a plain or a flat tableland. Here it
refers to the plateau between the Arnon River and the city of Heshbon (cf. Deut. 4:43; Josh. 13:9,16,17,21; Jer. 48:8,21). This
plateau was part of Moab and became the tribal inheritance of Reuben (cf. Josh. 20:8).

▣ "Gilead" The term (BDB 166) is of unknown origin or meaning. A popular (word play) definition
is given in Gen. 31:48. It can refer to:

- a tribe (e.g. Num. 26:29; Jdg. 5:17)

- a land (e.g. Gen. 37:25)

It always refers to an area on the east side of the Jordan River from the Arnon River north to the land of Bashan.

▣ "Salecah" This city (BDB 699) seems to form the southeastern limit of Bashan and is often used, along with
Mt. Hermon, to designate the extent of Bashan (cf. Josh. 12:5; 13:11; 1 Chr. 5:11).

3:11 This seems to be an editorial comment, like Deut. 2:10-12,20; 3:9.

▣ "Rephaim" This can mean

- an ethnic group

- giants

- the realm of the dead

The context here seems to speak of the giants.

The term (BDB 793) basically means "a wooden frame." It could be used of a trellis, couch,
bed, saddle, chair/throne. Here it refers to a place to sleep. At this period iron was new and precious.

- bed ‒ 2 Sam. 17:28; Job 7:13; Ps. 6:6; 41:3; Amos 6:4

- couch ‒ Prov. 7:16

- coffin (sarcophagus, i.e. one's final place of rest/sleep)

It is possible that "iron" refers to basalt stone sarcophagus color (cf. NET Bible, p. 350). NIDOTTE,
vol. 1, p. 741, says, "there is no literary support for the suggestion this was a sarcophagus or dolmen."

▣ "Rabbah" This (BDB 913) was the capital of the kingdom of Ammon (cf. Josh. 13:25). It is today the capital of Jordan, Amman.

▣ "an ordinary cubit" This is literally, "to the cubit of a man," which was an idiom for a "standard cubit," not a "royal cubit."

This measurement would make the bed 13' by 6'.

3:12 "Reubenites and Gadites" These two tribes took over Sihons' kingdom (cf. Josh. 13:15-23,24-28).

3:13 "half-tribe" The two sons of Joseph made up the half-tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim (cf. Gen. 41:50,52; 48:1-7).
Manasseh's inheritance was split, half on the eastern side of Jordan and half on the western side.

3:14 "Jair" Rather than "son of" this means "descendant of" (cf. Num. 32:41). Several of the generations are

Craigie, p. 121).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ."

▣ "the son of Manasseh" "Son" here means descendant rather than direct son (cf. 1 Chr. 2:22).

▣ "Geshurites and Maachathites" These are different racial and ethnic groups (BDB 178 and BDB 591). They
lived on the northern border of the land of Bashan (cf. Josh. 13:13). Israel did not fight these people.

▣ "Havoth-jair" This can refer to a "town," "region," or "kingdom" (BDB 795 II) of Jair.

▣ "as it is to this day" This phrase refers to a later period than the event (cf. Deut. 2:22; 3:14; 4:38;
10:8,15; 29:28; Josh. 7:26; 8:28,29; 9:27; 13:13; 14:14; 16:10; 22:3,17; 23:8; Jdg. 1:21,26; 10:4; 18:12,30; 19:30). Verse 5 seems
to have a similar thrust. The issue is "how much" later. It can refer to "soon after" (e.g. Josh. 6:25; 23:9) or it can mean
generations later. Who recorded Moses words? Who arranged the Pentateuch? Who was the final editor? Modern
scholarship cannot answer these questions!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PENTATEUCH

3:15 "To Machir" Numbers 32:39-40 gives more information about this man.

3:17 "Arabah" This was another word for the Jordan Valley, which goes from above the Sea of Galilee past the
Dead Sea down to the Gulf of Aqaba in the Sinai Peninsula (see note at Deut. 1:1). This is a geological rift through
which the Jordan River runs, from the foothills of Mt. Hermon to the Dead Sea.

▣ "Chinnereth" This (BDB 490) is the name of a city in Galilee which was close to a large lake that
goes by several names in the Bible:

- Chinnereth (e.g. Num. 34:11; Josh. 12:3; 13:27)

- Galilee (e.g. Matt. 4:18; Mark 1:16; John 6:1)

- Gennesaret (e.g. Luke 5:1)

- Tiberias (e.g. John 6:1; 21:1)

▣ "the sea of the Arabah" This lake (cf. Deut. 4:49; Josh. 3:16; 12:3) is also called

- "Sea of the Plain" in 2 Kgs. 14:25 is another name for the Salt Sea (cf. Gen. 14:3; Num. 34:3,12;
Josh. 3:16; 15:2,5; 18:19)

- as it is called today, the Dead Sea

- "the eastern sea" (cf. Ezek. 47:18; Joel 2:20; Zech. 14:8)

- just "the sea" (cf. Isa. 16:8; Jer. 48:32)

▣ "Pisgah" This mountain (BDB 820) is identified with or is very close to Mt. Nebo (BDB 612 I, cf.
Deut. 32:49; 34:1). Possibly they are twin peaks of one formation or the name of the ridge and its highest peak. These
mountains are the result of erosion of the plateau of Moab above the Arabah. This name is more common in the OT
than Nebo (cf. Num. 21:20; 23:14; Deut. 3:17,27; 4:49; 34:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "shall cross over armed before your brothers" Because Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled on
the eastern side of the Jordan which had already been conquered, their young men were now to go into battle first and fight for their
brothers' land (cf. Deut. 3:19-20) before they could settle in their own land.

▣ "sons of Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

3:19 "much livestock" The "much livestock" which they had were the spoils of war both from

- Egypt

- the trans-Jordan nations

▣ "which I have given you" The source of all blessings is YHWH (the often used VERB "given," BDB 678,
KB 733, Qal PERFECT). They had not earned the spoils of war themselves.

3:20 "the Lord gives rest to your fellow countrymen" The book of Hebrews is the best
NT commentary on the Pentateuch. In Hebrews 4, the word "rest" is used three ways:

- a seventh day rest as God rested after creation, the Sabbath

- the Israelites rested after they conquered the Promised Land (cf. Deut. 12:10; 25:19; Josh. 23:1)

- heaven, the eternal seventh-day rest

Here "rest" refers to security, #2.

3:21 Because of YHWH's provision in the wilderness and victories in the trans-Jordan, the Israelis are
to trust Him and march on!

▣ "Joshua" This man became Moses' trusted helper and military leader. His name (BDB 221) in Hebrew
is a combination of "YHWH" and "save." A VERB must be added, "YHWH saves," "YHWH brings salvation,"
"salvation is of YHWH." The Aramaic form of this name is "Jesus."

Apparently he was originally called "Hoshea" (cf. Deut. 32:44), but later the abbreviation for the covenant
name for Israel's deity, "YHWH," was prefixed.

3:22 "the Lord your God is the one fighting for you" This is not human effort, skills,
or resources, but God's power (cf. Deut. 1:30; 20:4; Exod. 14:14; 15:3).

▣ "for what god is there in heaven or earth who can do such works and mighty acts as Yours" Is this the
concept that YHWH is the supreme God among many other spiritual beings, called henotheism (e.g. Exod. 15:11 and Deut. 4:7; 5:7)?
Does this mean that

- Moses is affirming the existence of other gods (i.e. elohim)

- however, YHWH is the strongest

- Or is this monotheism (e.g. Deut. 4:35,39; 6:4; Exod. 20:2-3; Isa. 43:11; 44:6,8,24; 45:5,6-7,14,18,21,22), one and only one God?

We really do not know. I would rather believe that Moses is not referring to other gods, but to other

3:26 "the Lord was angry" This is an example of anthropomorphic language
("angry" BDB 720, KB 780). How can we express God's being upset without using human terms? We can't, but we must
remember that God is not a human and does not think and act like humans (i.e. Isa. 55:9-11). We use human terms to describe
the nature of God knowing that fallen humans can not ultimately describe God.

Moses' public sin (cf. Deut. 32:51; Num. 20:10-12; 27:12-14) brought public consequences!

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own

the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.
